job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior operations analyst at a payments start-up in Lisbon, about sixty people. I studied economics, passed with a plain result, no internships, and got the job four months ago through a friend's cousin. Most days I clean transaction data, build dashboards and chase failed payments, and I have an AI assistant open in a window all day. I share a flat with a Brazilian designer and a Polish engineer. Evenings I tinker with side scripts, or go to a climbing gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it would be a bit of a letdown. I use AI every day to write queries and tidy data, and it saves me maybe an hour. I'd tell friends it's a good tool that doesn't change the world, and online I'd probably stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge shrinks a little. If everyone has the same tool, being good with it isn't special any more. But I'd still be fine, because the start-up needs people who can think about the data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. I'd keep my job, keep saving about 400 a month, and spend my evenings learning proper statistics instead of tool tricks. I'd also keep hunting for things at work that nobody has automated yet, because that's how I get noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly flat, to be honest, because I'm riding the wave and I'd like it to be bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is the start-up itself. We raised money last year, and if the next round doesn't come the company could fold. Then I'd be out in a market full of other juniors, though I'd have savings, about twelve thousand, to survive on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly investors who treat start-ups like lottery tickets. Also the cost of living in Lisbon, which pushes everyone my age into sharing. I don't blame the technology.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** that doesn't change the world.
I'd stay out of the online argument.
think: If everyone has the same tool, being good with it isn't **special** any more.
The start-up still needs people who can **think** about data.
do: Keep saving **400 a month** and learn proper **statistics** in the evenings.
Look for tasks at work nobody has automated yet.
feel: **Calm**, slightly flat because I'd like the wave bigger.
S0.quote: If everyone has the same tool, being good with it isn't special any more.
fieldNote: **Adaptive** and curious: even a quiet scenario makes him plan his next skill.
Mood is uneasy because the **start-up** may fold, not because of AI.
Blames investors and city costs, not technology.

steps.text: Learn proper statistics in the evenings
Save 400 a month toward a rainy-day fund
Find tasks at work nobody has automated yet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and rough at once. I'd say to my team that the people who can direct the tools will do well, and I'd help others at the start-up get started. Online, I'd probably post what I've learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of what a junior analyst does gets taken first. Cleaning data and building dashboards is what I do, and my assistant already does half of it. So I need to move up to the thinking part quickly, before a junior hire isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my work toward working out what the numbers mean, talk to customers, and learn how to build small automations. I'd ask my boss for a project that's mine. I'd also put out a small portfolio of what I've built, in case I need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped but nervous. It's a race, and I like races, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't checking the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dashboards, honestly. I've already built three, and I can now get the assistant to build one in twenty minutes. My boss would notice because the weekly report would arrive on Monday morning rather than Wednesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a budget to buy tools and courses, and for each junior to own a project with a real customer. I'd also want honesty. If the company plans to hire fewer analysts, tell us.

say: I'd say it's **exciting and rough** at once, and tell my team to learn to direct the tools.
I'd share what I learn online and help colleagues start.
think: Cleaning data and building dashboards is what I do, and it's what gets **taken first**.
I need to move up to the **thinking part** quickly.
do: Shift to **interpreting** numbers, talk to customers and build small automations.
Ask my boss for a **project of my own** and publish a small portfolio.
feel: **Pumped but nervous**, because it's a race.
S1.quote: Cleaning data and building dashboards is what I do, and my assistant already does half of it.
fieldNote: He reads the scenario as a **race** and wants to be early.
Honest that his own entry-level tasks are the exposed ones.
Plans a portfolio as insurance, a very **adaptive** move.

steps.text: Ask my boss for a customer project of my own
Build three small automations for the operations team
Publish a portfolio of my dashboards and scripts
Take a course in data interpretation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's insane and it's coming too fast. I'd say we need governments to set up something like a basic income, a tax on the AI companies, and training that actually works. I'd probably be on the call-in shows of my friends' podcasts saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried but also kind of wired. Two years isn't enough for me to become a senior anything, so I'd be competing with the machine as a junior. But I'm the type who learns the tools first, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd tell my boss I want to be the one working with the AI systems. I'd put savings of about fourteen thousand into something safe and cut my spending, no more climbing gym membership. I'd also look for a role at an AI company or one that deploys it, because that's where the work might be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a jolt of adrenaline. I can't pretend I'm not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start building something small of my own, a tool I could sell to small businesses. If it works, great. If it doesn't, I'd have proof I can build, which helps me get hired anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents it's serious, and that I'm acting rather than waiting. I'd leave out the possibility that I can't pay my share of the rent in a year.

say: I'd say it's **insane** and governments need a basic income and a tax on AI firms.
I'd say it on friends' podcasts.
think: Two years isn't enough to become senior, so I'd compete with the machine as a **junior**.
Still, learning tools first is a real **edge**.
do: Tell my boss I want to work with the **AI systems** and cut spending.
Start building a small **tool** to sell to small businesses.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough for me to become a senior anything, so I'd be competing with the machine as a junior.
fieldNote: Anxious but **energised**: acts quickly instead of freezing.
Side project is both income plan and proof of skill.
Hides his rent fear from his **parents**.

steps.text: Ask my boss to put me on the AI systems team
Cancel the climbing gym and trim spending
Build a small tool to sell to local businesses
Move savings into a safe account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, just calmer. I'd say five years is a real chance if we don't waste it. I'd be loud about retraining funds and about companies being open on how many people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lets me get seriously good. I'd be twenty-seven, with the experience to move into a role that directs AI systems. The danger is if I stay a button-presser and everyone else has caught up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd move to a bigger firm or a team that builds the tools, not just uses them. I'd learn Python properly and take a part-time master's in data science or finance. And I'd set aside a growing share of salary, maybe 600 a month, since a long bad patch could follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. It feels like there's something to do with the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd go for depth. In two years the best I could do is scramble and hope. With five I could actually earn a name for something, maybe in a niche like fraud analytics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings first, then the master's, then maybe a small share in a start-up of a friend's. I'd keep a safety fund of six months of expenses always, because careers don't move in straight lines.

say: I'd say five years is a **real chance** and push for retraining funds.
I'd say companies should be open about how many people they replace.
think: Five years lets me get **seriously good** and move to a role that directs AI.
do: Move to a team that **builds** tools and learn Python properly.
Start a part-time **master's** and save 600 a month.
feel: **Uneasy** but fired up, with something to do with the time.
S3.quote: With five I could actually earn a name for something, maybe in a niche like fraud analytics.
fieldNote: Time turns into a **depth** strategy rather than a scramble.
Plans the master's and bigger savings in parallel.
Keeps a six-month safety fund as a **rule**.

steps.text: Move to a team that builds AI tools
Take a part-time master's in data science
Learn Python properly and publish projects

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have plenty of time and still probably won't use it well. I'd say it's like climate change: lots of talk, slow action. I'd be one of the people pushing for early rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a lot of runway. I'd be thirty-two, and I could be leading a team or running my own company. By then the people who understood these tools early will be the ones everyone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, finish a master's, build a side business, and invest part of my salary. I'd also move across to a firm building AI products, probably abroad. It wouldn't feel like a gamble because I'd have a decade to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and kind of excited. It's the version where being curious pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build a company properly, with savings and experience behind it. In two years I'd have nothing to lean on but luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be building things, not just analysing. Maybe a company that helps small firms use these tools. I'd still care about who gets left behind, so I'd want it to be fair.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and we still probably won't use it well.
I'd be pushing for early rules.
think: Ten years is a lot of **runway**, and I could be leading or running my own company.
People who understood the tools early will be the ones **everyone calls**.

Move to a firm building **AI products**, maybe abroad.
feel: **Calm** and excited, the version where curiosity pays.

fieldNote: Longest runway pushes him from employee to **builder**.
Still cares about fairness, which keeps him out of pure self-interest.
Willing to take **risk** because there's time to recover.

steps.text: Finish a master's and build a side business
Invest part of every salary in index funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can handle a lot, but two years is too short to build savings, skills and a reputation together. What would help is a basic safety net, training I can fit around work, and being honest from employers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age aren't afraid of the tools, we're afraid of being treated as disposable. That's the thing nobody asks.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't afraid of the tools, we're afraid of being treated as disposable.
portrait: Victor is 22, a junior operations analyst at a Lisbon payments start-up, four months into his first job.
He uses an AI assistant all day and is the one friends ask to show them the tools.
His outlook leans progressive: he wants basic income, taxes on AI firms and honest employers.
With twelve thousand saved and a start-up that might fold, he moves between **calm** and anxious, acting early in each.
Given more time he becomes a builder, with side tools, a master's and perhaps his own company.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries him most, because skills, savings and reputation can't all be built in time.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **basic safety net**, training that fits around work and honesty from employers.
